#4697. Rare rhino birth caught on camera at England’s Chester Zoo

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 7:01 PM EST

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been announced yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”

#4696. Does Black Friday Make Everything Else Seem Expensive?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

There is something rather irritating about seeing a product heavily discounted during the Black Friday sales, only to see it back at full price a few days later. Before the sale, the original price might have seemed perfectly reasonable. But once the excitement of the sale has died down, it feels expensive, and paying the full price seems almost painful.

Black Friday discounts might do more than encourage us to spend money during the sales. They could also change our perception of value and how much we're willing to pay for things long after the bargains have disappeared.

When we buy something, we tend to think that we're making a rational judgment about whether it's worth the price. But how do we decide what something is actually worth?

One way is by comparing the asking price with what we've paid before or what we've seen the product selling for elsewhere. This gives us what is known as a reference price, a sort of benchmark we use to decide whether something seems expensive or cheap.

Over time, and after many repeated purchases, we become accustomed to paying a certain amount for a particular product. We accept that amount as its normal price, and it becomes what we expect to pay. But then Black Friday happens, which nowadays may last for a full month rather than one day, and that same product is suddenly available for considerably less.

Even though we know perfectly well that the discount is temporary, that lower price starts to influence what we think the product should cost. It can become a new reference point against which we judge future prices.

When the sale ends and the price returns to normal, the amount we have become used to paying no longer seems quite so reasonable. The deal has changed our perception of value.

When a discount changes what we think something is worth, it can also change whether we're willing to buy it at all.

Across three studies, Guo (2026) found that consumers who had seen an extremely low price were less willing to buy the same product later at a higher price than those who had seen a smaller discount. What was interesting was why they didn't want to buy it.

Seeing the lower price reduced how much participants thought the product was worth. The prospect of paying the higher price also increased their anticipated regret. They expected to feel worse about buying something they knew had previously been priced for considerably less.

It didn't matter whether participants had previously bought the product at the cheaper price. Simply knowing it had once been available for less was enough to discourage a future purchase. We don't necessarily have to miss out on a bargain for it to change our perception of value, which the researcher called the postdiscount effect.

The findings raise an interesting question about Black Friday. If retailers spend weeks convincing us that their products are worth buying at heavily discounted prices, what happens when they expect us to start paying full price again?

This is where Black Friday might become a problem for retailers themselves. Black Friday is designed to encourage us to buy more by making products temporarily cheaper. But in doing so, retailers may also be changing what we're willing to pay for those products in the future. They could be inadvertently teaching us that their products are worth less than they originally claimed.

The more accustomed we become to seeing discounts, the more we might begin questioning whether the full price is ever worth paying. Why buy something today when it might be cheaper again next month in the post-Christmas sales? Why pay the normal price when we've seen exactly how little a retailer was prepared to sell it for last week?

There's nothing wrong with taking advantage of a good Black Friday discount. You've made a sensible decision if you've been planning to buy something and find it cheaper. The problem is when we allow that temporary price to determine what we think something should cost long after the sales have finished.

That's the irony of Black Friday. Retailers spend much of November getting us excited and convincing us that we're going to get extraordinary value for our money. In doing so, they might also be convincing us that their products were never worth the original asking price.

They may have saved us money today, but they've made everything seem more expensive tomorrow.

Guo, T. (2026). From inaction inertia to the postdiscount effect: How a lower price reduces subsequent purchase after it expires. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 39(4), e70092

We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

#4692. Zines Are a Great Tool for Learning

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

A zine (pronounced “zeen”) is a little booklet or mini-magazine you make yourself, combining elements of a scrapbook, journal, collage, or a handmade book. You can write, draw, add photos, stickers, quotes, stories, or anything else you want to express. Everything is customizable, from page size and arrangement to colors, materials, and overall look and feel. Zines have a long history of giving people excluded from mainstream publishing a way to share their ideas, experiences, art, and perspectives. Today, zine-making is a worldwide culture, with makers sharing and trading their work at fairs, festivals, libraries, bookstores, and community spaces. The zine has become a cultural icon with a distinct history, community, and spirit of creative independence.

Zine-making is a form of project-based learning and a student-centered way of learning through creating something meaningful. Project-based learning gives people an active role: they explore questions, solve problems, make choices, connect ideas, and apply what they are learning to real situations. Zines bring some especially useful qualities to that process. They give people many ways to work with an idea through writing, images, collage, humor, stories, symbols, personal experience, or cultural references, while also asking them to think about who will read or see the zine and how they want to communicate with that audience. The finished zine becomes something they can hold, share, discuss, and return to later. Across studies in classrooms and museums, zine-making has helped people connect course or exhibit content with their own experiences and interests, while giving them space to shape that learning into something distinctly their own.

Psychologically, making a zine brings together what a person notices, remembers, feels, experiences, questions, and connects while they are actively making something. As they revisit what they know, new information connects with prior experience and can reshape how they understand it. Putting ideas into words, images, and materials makes those ideas visible, giving the person something to reconsider and change. Thinking about an audience shapes how they communicate, while reflection can also turn inward toward identity and belief. Through this process, people build knowledge that feels meaningful and personal.

In this zine, the maker transforms a museum visit into a reflection on love, connection, memory, and being alive. Using photographs from the visit, handwritten thoughts, museum materials, collage, thread, and a three-dimensional heart labeled “my core,” they connect dinosaurs, animals, ancient history, memory, and emotion through themes of love and interconnectedness. Museum content becomes part of a personal interpretation, helping the maker explore what the visit means to them and communicate that meaning to others.

In this zine, a student transforms educational psychology concepts into a personal explanation of learning. They use gears to represent thinking, a bell for behavior and conditioning, drawings of memory and motivation, and a child connecting ideas across the page. They also develop their own argument that creativity is a form of intelligence, extending the course material with a personal claim. By choosing how to connect and visually represent these concepts, the student creates both a reflection on their learning and an expression of how they understand education.

Zine-making is accessible almost anywhere, from homes and classrooms to museums and community spaces, using simple materials like paper, pens, magazines, photos, and stickers.

Anyone can make a zine, so give it a try and see what emerges!

April Ursula Fox, Ph.D. (UNLV), is an educational psychology teacher and researcher whose work explores learner agency, multimodal learning, and applied educational psychology across formal and informal learning environments.

#4691. Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated plan of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health issues can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

They stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” said Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these new reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

She said issues with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg said.

Suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” said Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are important windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” said William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

The authors of that report listed several steps they said could reverse these trends. Among them:

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu said.

Weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”

#4690. Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a new electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

The VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously said the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

When I teach positive psychology, a topic students are interested in is “What makes us happy?” What actions can we take to increase our experience of psychological well-being? I’ll start with the bottom line: Research consistently shows that experiences make us much happier (and for longer) than material items (TV, sofa, a gadget).

5. Chan and Mogilner (2016) ran four studies and found that experiential gifts strengthen the bond between giver and recipient more than material ones. #4687. Rinnai’s new heat pump water heaters get smarter – and easier to install

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

The REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

#4685. How to Maneuver Generational Differences Over the Holidays

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

With the holidays yet again upon us, people will be setting their holiday gathering plans and preparing for an onslaught of multi-generational togetherness. When coming together for the holidays, the goal isn’t necessarily for everyone to think or celebrate alike; it’s to celebrate harmony and happiness while making room for the differences that you know may come with getting so many people of varying ages together in one room.

Here, we discuss how to make room at one’s table for generational differences while protecting the deep thread of connection that makes everyone family.

We’ve all experienced it. The sideways glances at the child who won’t eat their turkey. The sighs and stories about “Back in my day…” The admonishment to the teenager to “put your phone away.” The mom in the middle of it all who just wants a group photo of everyone before they dig in.

These are the sights and sounds of most holiday family gatherings. The younger generation has taken over the planning and organization of events, while the older generation sits in the wake of it all, wondering why anything had to change.

Even though the holidays bring together people who love one another, they can also bring friction. According to a 2023 American Psychological Association poll, 89% of U.S. adults reported holiday-related stress, and 22% identified the experience or anticipation of family conflict as a source of that stress.

However, generational differences don’t have to derail a holiday gathering. Once we learn to stop anticipating conflict and start remembering the reason we get together in the first place, we can begin looking forward to the fun stories, skill sharing, and memory-making that make the holidays so special.

It can be easy to get immediately annoyed when Grandpa starts talking about how they used to discipline kids or Great Aunt Margaret says that your stuffing was made incorrectly. Try to reframe statements before irritation or misunderstandings get out of control.

For example, instead of getting bothered when an older member of the family admonishes a child for being on their device, think about why they may be mentioning it. Perhaps they want to spend more time talking with the child, or maybe there are some cultural expectations around the holidays at play.

Researchers found that interactions and education can reduce or even eliminate ageism, which can be at play during multi-generational events. By teaching the younger generation about aging and helping them connect with older people, you can eliminate miscommunication, fear, and negative feelings.

Laying out expectations and boundaries can also be an effective way to help the holiday get-together go more smoothly between the generations. Prior to the event, invite the older generations into a conversation about plans. This way, there will be less chance of surprise or disappointment, and the older generation family members will feel like they are contributing.

Take care to ask about meaningful traditions in the family and choose a few to carry on while leaving room for something new. Discuss important topics like gift budgets, transportation, locations, and food options before the holidays so that there is less room for conflict.

Boundaries can sometimes sound like a dirty word to older generations, but they can still be important for intergenerational harmony during the holidays. First, distinguish between what you are willing to compromise on to keep the peace and a personal boundary that absolutely must be respected.

For example, letting Grandma tell stories about her childhood on the farm may not necessarily hurt anyone, but comments about your body, children declining a hug from a relative, or politics may be in need of some boundary-setting intervention. If boundaries that are important to you are repeatedly ignored, have a place you can go to take a break or a code word with your partner to signal that you need some help getting out of a conversation.

When you get different generations of family together for the holiday, there is bound to be some friction. We live in increasingly divided times, and people may feel more comfortable around their family letting conflicting opinions fly. Holiday hosts should aim to connect the generations instead of steeling themselves for inevitable discourse.

The ultimate goal isn’t to resolve all differences and agree every step of the way (that’s likely impossible). Instead, families should make room for stories, laughter, and the kind of connection that’s only possible between people who know one another as well as family members do.

1. “Even a joyous holiday season can cause stress for most Americans”. (2023, November 30). American Psychological Association. Retrieved November 2, 2026, from https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/11/holiday-season-stress.

2. Burnes, D., Sheppard, C., Henderson, C. R., Wassel, M., Cope, R., Barber, C., & Pillemer, K. (2019). Interventions to reduce ageism against older adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Public Health, 109(8). https://doi.org/10.2105/ajph.2019.305123

#4684. Tesla Cybercab orders open at $29,990 + $299/mo, only in Robotaxi zones

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print says “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”

The rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

Railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” currently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, and it works anywhere, no geofence required. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4683. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

#4681. The Gift That Keeps on Giving

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I was running out to grab a cup of coffee and asked my co-worker if I could grab one for her. No biggie, just a common courtesy. I literally didn’t even go out of my way. But when I returned, she couldn't have been more grateful. Sometimes when we do small, simple things, we realize later how much they meant to others.

It could be something like a thoughtful message or a quick check-in where we take a few minutes to listen.

The thing is, we often underestimate the impact of these simple gestures. We are all so busy these days, caught up in daily responsibilities and checking all the boxes to complete everything on our list, that we tend to forget how much we can effortlessly offer to others.

Of course, in this fast-paced world, we are always striving for more from life. And, at the same time, it's important to pause and recognize what we have and how it can be shared with those around us.

Just take a moment to think about some of the people who make a difference in your life. Perhaps it was that friend who checked in on you during a difficult time or a supervisor who encouraged you. They may not have given their generosity much thought, but I bet you remember how it made you feel, right?

Let me share with you a research study that supports this idea. A 2023 study in the Journal of Experimental Psychology found that people frequently underestimate how positive acts of kindness impact others. In one study, participants who gave strangers hot chocolate thought the recipients would be happy, but in reality, the recipients were incredibly grateful for the gesture.

Generativity, a concept developed by psychologist Erik Erikson, describes how a person wants to contribute to the lives of others and make a difference for future generations. This is evidenced in the things that we do, like mentoring others, supporting a friend or family member, or sharing lessons.

It’s important to mention that the research demonstrates a strong connection between helping people and well-being. In 2020, Psychological Bulletin published a meta-analysis of more than 200 studies and found a consistent relationship between helping people and positive well-being.

It’s important to mention that giving to others doesn't mean we are neglecting our needs. It just means that we are also helping one another build relationships. And the research also shows that a sense of connection really matters.

Sadly, we are often so busy managing all that we have to do that we don't think about how we can support others.

Which of these options could you incorporate into your schedule this week? (Choose just one.) You will both benefit if you reach out, offer a little encouragement, listen, or just let someone know they are on your mind. The point is that it doesn't have to be this big grand gesture. Small acts of kindness go a long way.

Life's most meaningful moments happen with people who took the time to listen, remember, or encourage, or helped us feel less alone. Don’t wait for more time or money, or until you've figured everything out, before you try to make a difference. Just start with where you are.

Take a moment and think about one small act of kindness that was bestowed upon you. How can you do the same for others?

Erikson, E. H. (1950). Childhood and society. W. W. Norton.

Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: A meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316

Hui, B. P. H., Ng, J. C. K., Berzaghi, E., Cunningham-Amos, L. A., & Kogan, A. (2020). Rewards of kindness? A meta-analysis of the link between prosociality and well-being. Psychological Bulletin, 146(12), 1084–1116. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000298

Kumar, A., & Epley, N. (2023). A little good goes an unexpectedly long way: Underestimating the positive impact of kindness on recipients. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 152(1), 236–252. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001271

#4680. I finally got a USB-C charging e-bike, and it costs 75% less than Rivian’s bike

I’ve been waiting years for electric bikes to finally embrace USB-C charging. We’ve already standardized much of our lives around the convenient little connector, from phones and laptops to tablets and countless other gadgets. But for some reason, electric bikes have largely missed the memo. Now, though, I’m finally riding an e-bike that charges with USB-C, and the best part is that it doesn’t cost an arm and a leg.

Meet the ENGWE Zip, a quirky little folding electric bike that costs just €999 and has quickly become one of my favorite examples of how a small feature can make a big difference.

When it debuted earlier this year, it became only the third production e-bike I’ve seen that could charge via USB-C, allowing it to use the same charger that is likely already shared by your phone and laptop.

USB-C charging on electric bikes isn’t entirely new, but it’s surprisingly rare. Ampler was one of the first companies to introduce it barely a year ago, though its bikes are sadly no longer in production after the company’s bankruptcy. More recently, Rivian’s ALSO electric bike arrived with USB-C charging, but that bike costs around $4,500 – at least if you want the model that’s slowly starting to ship.

The ENGWE Zip, on the other hand, costs roughly a quarter as much as its only USB-charging competition. At €999, it’s priced at a relatively affordable US$1,100. That’s a quarter of the cost of the only other USB-C charging e-bike on the market.

Of course, it’s not nearly as technologically advanced as Rivian’s ALSO e-bike. But hey, it’s at least shipping.

And while the Zip is a fun little 16″ wheel folding electric bike in its own right, with a compact design that makes it easy to store and transport, it’s the charging setup that has me particularly excited.

Instead of keeping track of yet another proprietary charging brick, I can simply grab the USB-C charger from my laptop and plug it into the bike. There’s one in my living room by the couch. There’s one by my bed. There’s one in all of my friends’ places. There’s a USB-C charger everywhere.

If I’m traveling around, that means one less charger to pack. If I’m visiting someone, there’s a decent chance they already have a compatible charger sitting around.

Heck, I can even use a basic USB-C phone charger in a pinch. Sure, charging a relatively large e-bike battery at 20W isn’t going to be particularly quick, but the fact that I can do it at all is incredibly convenient.

Plus, the bike has one more trick. The battery also outputs USB-C, so I can charge my laptop or other devices from it as well. I can even charge two devices simultaneously, thanks to the dual USB-C ports.

The battery is housed in a roll-top bag that is locked into the headset of the bike but can be quickly unlocked for charging off the bike. And since it’s a keyed lock, no one can steal the battery even when the bag is left on the bike.

I typically charge the battery still mounted on the bike, though occasionally when I want to use a friend’s USB-C charger, I’ll just pop the bag off and bring it right up to wherever the closest USB-C charger is located.

It may not be the fastest charge, but it’s pretty darn convenient. And with a 360Wh battery, a powerful 100W laptop charger will still get it pretty much full in 4 hours, or for a more typical 50% recharge, roughly two hours.

And that’s really the beauty of USB-C charging. It’s not necessarily about charging faster. It’s about having options. It’s about not being stuck if the very specific charger that only works on your e-bike doesn’t happen to be around exactly where you are.

Of course, there’s a technical reason we haven’t seen USB-C charging spread across the e-bike industry quite as quickly as it has with smaller electronics. Most e-bike batteries operate at 36V or 48V nominal, meaning their charging voltages are higher than the 20V typically supplied by common USB-C laptop chargers. That requires additional voltage conversion and charging circuitry inside the bike or battery.

But clearly, it can be done. And if ENGWE can offer it on a €999 electric bike, there’s a pretty compelling argument that more manufacturers should be taking a serious look at the technology. In this case, it’s all housed inside the battery, meaning it could be directly incorporated into any e-bike whose manufacturer is brave enough to spec it.

USB-C charging aside, there's a very good reason that just about every folding e-bike on the market has put thick plates on the folding connection of the frame. It's because the frame breaks if they're not there. Just like this one is going to.

I’m not suggesting that every e-bike needs to abandon its dedicated charger tomorrow. For larger batteries, high-powered chargers still make plenty of sense, especially when you want to get back on the road quickly.

But having USB-C as an additional charging option? That’s something I’d love to see become standard.

For years, we’ve seen how electric bikes are becoming more convenient, more practical, and better integrated into our everyday lives. Yet when it comes to charging, we’re still carrying around a collection of more or less proprietary chargers.

Now I’m riding a barely $1k electric bike that can charge from the same power brick as my laptop. And frankly, I think it’s about time the rest of the e-bike industry caught up!

#4678. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#4677. 5 Things We’re Saying No to This Holiday Season

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Before you say yes this holiday season, ask yourself what you’re saying yes to. Consider the feelings that come up for you when you think about it. Is it excitement about seeing the people you love? Is it dread at the anticipation of planning, conflict, or grief? For some, it’s all of the above.

Recent polls find that nearly 9 in 10 (89%) U.S. adults report holiday stressors (APA, 2023). Tensions arise due to finances, family conflict, grief, and other factors. Stress takes away from the pleasurable aspects of the season, which should include reconnection and rest.

Sometimes that is easier said than done. Here are 5 things we're saying no to this holiday season and strategies to achieve the happy holidays we deserve.

Sometimes that family holiday announcement sounds like a demand rather than an invitation. “Dinner is at 4 pm sharp. See you there!” Everyone assumes you’ll be there, and no one asks questions. They don’t ask if you can take time off work, afford the trip, or have other plans. You feel obligated to attend despite any barriers you are facing.

Almost no one will tell you that you are allowed to consider your own needs before you RSVP yes. Ask yourself whether you have the time, energy, and money to participate this year. If the answer is no, it’s alright. Your family may be disappointed, and you may feel a little guilty, but it’s worth asking which will weigh on you more: the guilt of saying no or the cost of saying yes.

In toxic families, it’s the once-over as soon as you enter the room. Before you’ve even had a chance to sit down, someone has made a joke about your weight or graying hair, offered a backhanded compliment about the dish you contributed, or slipped in a dig about your personal life.

You may feel hurt, sad, or even angry, and you don’t have to ignore those feelings to preserve the holiday spirit. You can be silent and stone-faced to let the “joke” fall flat. You might excuse yourself and regroup in another room. If you want to address it directly and call out the hidden meaning, you can say, “That felt like a dig,” or ask, “What do you mean by that?” What you don’t have to do is tolerate disrespect.

When you want everyone to feel loved, it’s easy to slip into spending more than you intended. If you’ve ever hosted a large family gathering, you know how quickly the groceries and gifts add up. And if you’re the one who hosts every year, it can feel like the work and the bill are yours by default.

Before you do anything, set a budget. Then share the work in ways that play into everyone’s strengths. Maybe enlist the nephew who can roast meat or the cousin who loves to bake, and assign cleanup to the one you prefer to stay out of the kitchen. Suggest rotating hosting duties. Do a gift exchange rather than buying individual gifts for everyone. You can show your love to your family with limits.

In some families, playing the dutiful daughter (or son) means everyone assumes you’ll make the holidays happen. Often it’s the family matriarch or the eldest daughter who initiates the first call about the holiday plans and is the one still in the kitchen long after everyone else has gone home. She is the family “glue” who keeps track of the invites, remembers who can’t eat what, and figures out where to seat the relatives who aren’t speaking. By the time the holiday arrives, she’s too tired to enjoy the fruits of her labor.

If that sounds like you, name it. People who have never hosted may not realize all of the hidden effort that goes into an event. Bring it to their attention. Set limits on what you will do and ask for help, but don’t micromanage. If the person assigned to bring the rolls forgets, skip the rolls this year. If no one steps up, step back anyway. Plan a smaller, more intimate gathering that won’t leave you frazzled at the end of it.

The holidays aren’t the same after you’ve lost a loved one, and the first holiday season after a loss can be especially difficult. Family traditions may be upended. The person who always hosted and made everyone’s favorite dish is gone. Tensions that surface after the loss may still be hanging in the air.

Take a moment to evaluate your feelings. Ask yourself what you feel up to this year. Maybe it’s not the year to take on hosting duties, or perhaps you stop by for dessert rather than staying the entire day. You can choose to honor your loved one by retaining old traditions or step into the next chapter with new traditions in their memory. You can miss someone deeply and still make room for moments of joy this holiday season.

It might seem strange that saying no could be the start of a happy holiday. The beauty is that you get to decide what a happy holiday looks like for you, and that it can change from year to year. Ask yourself what would make the holidays feel good to you this year and do it.

American Psychological Association. (2023). Even a joyous holiday season can cause stress for most Americans. https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2023/11/holiday-season-stress

#4676. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output.
